title: Why data analysis without data quality is a healthcare risk
source_title: New WHO report reveals critical gaps in Africa's health information systems
evidence_type: WHO regional health information systems assessment announcement
evidence_status: Descriptive country-level capacity findings — not evidence of intervention impact
mode: Editorially prepared teaching case · fact and inference separated
research_depth: A source-linked educational review; the original WHO report is cited but has not been independently re-extracted in this editorial record
what_happened: A WHO assessment of health information systems across 40 countries in its African Region reported uneven health information system maturity and substantial gaps in facility-level data analysis and assessment of data quality.
before: The assessment documents existing capacity gaps. It does not describe one shared historical paper-based process for all 40 countries, nor a single intervention that has replaced that process.
what_changed: The new development is the publication of a regional assessment highlighting where health information systems need strengthening. Publication of the report itself does not demonstrate that patient care or health outcomes have already improved.
evidence: About 43% of assessed countries reported adequate facility-level capability to analyze data, while 25% reported sufficient capability to assess its quality. The two percentages measure different abilities and do not establish precisely how many countries possess both. An inability to verify data quality is a risk to decision-making, not proof that every decision is incorrect.
limitations: These statistics do not describe the percentage of individual facilities capable of each task. We cannot calculate the overlap of the two groups or infer that 43% of healthcare decisions are unreliable. Independent country-level methods and implementation results are needed before attributing improvements to specific technologies.

vocabulary.meaning: The people, tools and processes needed to interpret data and identify meaningful patterns.
Checks that establish whether recorded information is complete, accurate, consistent and useful for a particular decision.
The entity represented by each record, such as a country, hospital, patient or report.
The total eligible or assessed population used to calculate a proportion.

metrics: Facility report completeness: expected monthly submissions received ÷ expected submissions
On-time reporting: submissions received before deadline ÷ expected submissions
Duplicate patient records: probable duplicate records ÷ total patient records
bi_lessons: Always identify the unit of analysis before building a chart. The WHO percentages describe countries' reported facility-level capacity, not 43% of patients or individual hospitals. Separate data-analysis capability from confidence in data quality and do not infer their overlap without country-level observations.
question: How would you design a reporting-quality scorecard that prevents a ministry from trusting a compelling dashboard built from incomplete or duplicated records?

analyst_exercise.business_question: Which reporting and quality-assessment gaps should be prioritized across a fictional network of facilities?
analyst_exercise.dataset_design: Create synthetic dim_country, dim_facility, dim_month and fact_report_quality tables with expected_reports, received_reports, late_reports and duplicate_records.
analyst_exercise.data_quality_check: Check missing facilities, duplicates, denominator consistency, reporting periods and sample coverage.
analyst_exercise.power_bi_deliverable: Build a facility-quality dashboard with completeness, timeliness, duplicate rate and clearly displayed data-quality warnings.
analyst_exercise.sql_practice: GROUP BY facility_id and reporting_month. Calculate reporting completeness using received_reports / NULLIF(expected_reports,0), without treating missing facilities as zero errors.

title: Rwanda: From disconnected reporting to a national Health Intelligence Center
source: Rwanda Ministry of Health and NHIC Engineering Library
evidence_type: Official government platform and engineering documentation
evidence_status: Documented architecture and launch; downstream health-outcome improvements not independently established
mode: Editorially prepared multi-source case study · implementation versus outcome distinguished
research_depth: Government technical documentation, ministry announcement and implementation-partner account
what_happened: Rwanda launched its National Health Intelligence Center in April 2025. Official documentation describes a platform bringing information from nine national health information systems into a unified environment for analytics and decision-making. The engineering documentation describes API-driven pipelines and staging/validation architecture.
before: Rwanda already operated DHIS2 and other digital systems, but information across health programmes could remain fragmented. An implementation-partner account describes previous end-of-month manual reporting and consolidation taking days in some settings. This historical description is not proof that every facility worked identically.
what_changed: The national platform integrates routine reporting, community, disease surveillance and other sources. According to NHIC engineering documentation, Prefect pipelines retrieve data via REST APIs and land raw records in PostgreSQL staging tables, after which unified analytical models and validation processes support dashboards.
evidence: The April 2025 ministry launch and NHIC documentation establish the platform's existence and architecture. They do not alone demonstrate specific reductions in mortality, nationwide reporting errors or clinical waiting times. Claims of operational efficiency from implementation partners need independent baseline-to-follow-up measurement.
limitations: A national dashboard does not guarantee that every contributing source is complete or current. Before attributing better outcomes to NHIC, obtain platform coverage, pipeline uptime, source-data completeness, quality-audit results and measured changes in management decisions.

vocabulary.meaning: The ability of separate health information systems to exchange and use data.
Processes for extracting, loading and transforming information from operational systems into analytics-ready data.
An intermediate table containing imported source records before validation or modelling.
A traceable record of where a dashboard number came from and how it was transformed.

metrics: Data refresh latency: time between source event and availability in analytics layer
Source completeness: required records received ÷ required records expected
Reconciliation error rate: mismatched values between source and unified warehouse ÷ records checked
bi_lessons: Rwanda provides a realistic example of health data engineering as the foundation of trustworthy BI. Learn to design ingestion, staging, validation, transformation and visualization layers; identify whether a system is genuinely real-time or batch-updated. Always retain data provenance.
question: How would you validate a national disease surveillance chart if one district has stopped sending reports?

analyst_exercise.business_question: Which public-health programmes supply accurate and timely information to the national intelligence platform?
analyst_exercise.dataset_design: Using fictional data, build dim_program, dim_facility, dim_date, fact_extract_run and fact_validation_error; keep staging and curated data separate.
analyst_exercise.data_quality_check: Check null facility identifiers, missing reporting periods, duplicate feeds, failed API requests, reconciliation mismatches and freshness lag.
analyst_exercise.power_bi_deliverable: Design a source health dashboard showing refresh success, field completeness, pipeline latency and discrepancies by system and district.
analyst_exercise.sql_practice: Use ROW_NUMBER to detect repeat extracts per facility and month; compute current-to-source reconciliation by dataset and reporting period.

title: Kenya: Building a Shared Health Record that can follow patients
source_title: National Shared Health Record and FHIR patient summary
evidence_type: Official implementation standards and patient-record platform documentation
evidence_status: National standards and infrastructure documented; complete nationwide interoperability and outcome benefits not established
mode: Editorially prepared multi-source case study · interoperability lesson
research_depth: Official Digital Health Agency documentation, FHIR implementation guides and legal framework
what_happened: Kenya's Digital Health Agency is developing a national Health Information Exchange and Shared Health Record. Its official implementation guides specify structured patient summaries and a FHIR-based exchange approach to support the movement of clinical information across systems.
before: Kenya used separate systems such as KHIS/DHIS2 for routine reporting, KenyaEMR for HIV care, and community information applications. The Digital Health Agency's background guidance describes why this fragmented landscape needed interoperability. A patient's complete history was not necessarily available wherever they sought care.
what_changed: The Health Information Exchange provides shared components, including patient and facility registries, terminology, interoperable APIs and a Shared Health Record. Official guidance documents the mapping of patient summary resources and APIs for exchanging FHIR bundles. Authorized access and privacy safeguards are necessary.
evidence: Official digital health standards and implementation guides demonstrate a defined architecture and governance programme. Publishing standards or connecting some systems does not prove that every provider can see every patient record or that repeat testing has fallen nationally.
limitations: Challenges include reliable patient matching, quality of source EHR data, consent, security, rural connectivity, integration cost and actual adoption by facilities. Service outcomes require measured baselines, not only records of system deployment.

vocabulary.meaning: An HL7 standard describing structured healthcare resources and ways systems exchange them.
A coordinated longitudinal record designed to make relevant patient information accessible across participating care settings.
A standardized minimum set of clinically important patient information for continuity of care.
A registry or matching service designed to connect records belonging to the same individual across systems.

metrics: Successfully matched patient records ÷ cross-facility matching attempts
Relevant prior records retrievable during referrals ÷ referrals audited
Repeat laboratory tests within a defined clinical window ÷ eligible referred patients
bi_lessons: Interoperability is more than copying paper folders into software. Standardize identifiers, clinical terminology, date fields and resource schemas, then measure whether patient information actually moves securely between facilities and helps care teams.
question: What would you need to measure to show that a Shared Health Record reduced unnecessary repeat laboratory tests?

analyst_exercise.business_question: Can care providers retrieve relevant patient records across participating facilities without increasing privacy or duplicate-record risks?
analyst_exercise.dataset_design: Fictional dim_facility, dim_patient_pseudonym, dim_date, fact_record_request and fact_referral; use pseudonyms only.
analyst_exercise.data_quality_check: Assess patient matching errors, incomplete records, mismatched timestamps, authorization failures and duplicate patient identifiers.
analyst_exercise.power_bi_deliverable: Create a referral continuity dashboard comparing request success rates, record completeness, and median retrieval time by facility.
analyst_exercise.sql_practice: JOIN pseudonymized referrals to record-request events and calculate access success; avoid exposing identifying health details.

title: Nigeria: How Bauchi used community data to find children missed by vaccination services
source: Sabin Vaccine Institute; WHO Regional Office for Africa
source_title: Reaching Zero-Dose Children in Bauchi State, Nigeria
evidence_type: Documented community immunization project and related public-health reporting
evidence_status: 117 zero-dose and 181 defaulter children reached in a selected local project; national impact and mortality reduction not demonstrated
mode: Editorially prepared multi-source case study · service outputs distinguished from outcomes
research_depth: Project implementation account with additional WHO state-level reporting
what_happened: A community-led immunization tracking project in selected Bauchi State wards sought out children missed by routine services. Community registers, local dashboards and reconciliation with facility records were used to identify zero-dose children and children who had missed later vaccinations.
before: Routine facility data described doses delivered but could fail to fully identify children in settlements poorly reached by services. Caregivers could be waiting for vaccination teams; without community enumeration, some missing children were not adequately visible in facility reporting.
what_changed: Community volunteers and health teams used household line-listing, local registers, public community tracking boards and regular reconciliation with healthcare facilities. These lists supported outreach and follow-up rather than relying only on individuals appearing in routine facility datasets.
evidence: The Sabin case study reports 117 previously zero-dose children and 181 defaulters reached with vaccination through the tracking system in its target communities. These are documented service outputs for a specific intervention, not the number of children reached across Nigeria or proof of lower mortality.
limitations: A reported number reached does not prove complete population coverage, durable completion of all vaccine schedules, or impact on disease incidence. Population enumeration, catchment boundaries, comparison periods and continued follow-up are needed.

vocabulary.meaning: A child who has not received a first dose of an essential routine vaccine, frequently operationalized with DTP1.
A person who started but did not complete a scheduled vaccination or follow-up appointment within the expected interval.
Local planning that identifies eligible populations, settlements, service gaps and outreach actions.
Checking information across community registers and facility records to correct omissions and duplicates.

metrics: Zero-dose children newly reached ÷ eligible zero-dose children identified
Defaulters contacted and vaccinated ÷ defaulters identified
Community-register reconciliation coverage: settlements reconciled ÷ settlements targeted
bi_lessons: Reliable healthcare analytics must account for the people absent from facility records. A high-quality database of visitors can still miss entire communities. The relevant denominator is the eligible population, not just patients already seen.
question: If a project vaccinates 117 zero-dose children, what additional information is required to calculate coverage and determine whether the intervention reduced inequity?

analyst_exercise.business_question: Which communities contain the largest number of children not reached by routine immunization, and which follow-up actions are effective?
analyst_exercise.dataset_design: Create fictional dim_settlement, dim_child_pseudonym, dim_vaccine, fact_community_visit and fact_vaccination; separate identified children from completed doses.
analyst_exercise.data_quality_check: Check duplicated child records, missing settlements, inaccurate dates, inconsistent doses and children without home registration.
analyst_exercise.power_bi_deliverable: Build an outreach microplanning dashboard showing missing children, follow-up conversion, missed settlements and vaccine-stock availability.
analyst_exercise.sql_practice: LEFT JOIN community register against vaccination events to locate children with no documented first dose; calculate follow-up reach with a defined eligible denominator.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Digital Tools for Diabetes Self-management in Children: A Scoping Review.
source_title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Digital Tools for Diabetes Self-management in Children: A Scoping Review.
evidence_status: Measured improvement not established by the automated source review
mode: Research reading notes — not a verified impact study
what_happened: PubMed · Int J Endocrinol Metab published a primary-source record titled “Artificial Intelligence-Driven Digital Tools for Diabetes Self-management in Children: A Scoping Review..” The original article, abstract or registry entry was retrieved for study. Indexed research citation. Verify study design, sample, results and limitations in the original publication.
before: The available source metadata does not establish the exact prior workflow. To make a valid before-and-after comparison, review the publication and identify the setting, actors, existing processes and baseline metrics.
what_changed: The source identifies a research topic; verify the actual intervention and comparison group in the full paper before describing a change.
evidence: An indexed research citation is not enough to establish an effect. Read the methods, numerical results, and uncertainties in the primary paper.
limitations: No independent causal evaluation has been performed for this auto-generated briefing. Do not infer effectiveness, national scale-up or improvements in mortality from announcements, metadata or registrations.

vocabulary.meaning: The proportion of people with a condition correctly detected by a test or model.
The proportion of people without a condition correctly classified.
Testing a model using data from settings separate from development.

metrics: Sensitivity and specificity on independent clinical datasets
Median review turnaround time for eligible cases
False-alert rate in the intended use population
bi_lessons: Define the unit of analysis, baseline and denominator before interpreting this development. Propose KPIs relevant to the intervention and verify whether observed changes can be attributed to it.
question: What primary-source evidence would allow us to distinguish a promising announcement from a measurable improvement in healthcare delivery?
